## Subcomponents

### Section

Pairs a heading with collapsible content.
Use `defaultExpanded` to show the content initially.
Pass `onToggle` to be notified when the section opens or closes.

<Canvas of={AccordionSectionStories.Section} />

<Controls of={AccordionSectionStories.Section} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use an Accordion to keep secondary content collapsed by default, so the primary content of a page stays prominent.
A typical example is a list of frequently asked questions.

### When not to use

Don’t hide essential information in an Accordion.
Users may not realise it is there.

For long content that deserves its own page, split it across multiple pages instead.
That often improves both usability and findability through search engines.

### How to use

Use between 3 and 10 sections.
Fewer is rarely worth the extra interaction; more makes the list hard to scan.

Provide each section with a clear, descriptive label.
Users cannot scan the content inside a collapsed section.

Set `headingLevel` on the Accordion to match its position in the page hierarchy.
All sections share that level.

### How to write

Write labels that describe what the user will find inside the section.
Use sentence case.

## Examples

### Expanded by default

Pass `defaultExpanded` to a section to make it visible from the start.
Use this sparingly – it works against the goal of keeping content collapsed.

<Canvas of={AccordionStories.ExpandedByDefault} />

### Reduce landmarks

An Accordion Section renders a `<section>` element by default, which creates a landmark region.
Many landmarks on one page can be noisy for screen reader users.
For Accordions with six or more sections, render generic `<div>` elements through `sectionAs="div"`.

<Canvas of={AccordionStories.ReduceLandmarks} />

## Features

The Accordion provides the heading and the show-or-hide behaviour.
Section content can include formatted text, links, and other components.

### Keyboard navigation

| Key             | Behaviour                                                 |
| :-------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- |
| Enter or Space  | Open or close the focused section                         |
| Tab / Shift+Tab | Move to the next or previous focusable element            |
| Down / Up arrow | Move focus to the next or previous section (wraps around) |
| Home / End      | Move focus to the first or last section                   |

### Find in page

Browser ‘Find in page’ (Ctrl+F or ⌘+F) does not search inside collapsed sections.
If you can anticipate the search term, expand the relevant section automatically.

## Design

Section headings stay visible while their content collapses.
This lets users scan every section label without expanding anything.

Opening one section does not close the others.
A user looking for a specific answer can leave related context open as they explore.

The control is the heading rather than a button beside it.
The button fills the width of the heading and takes its typeface, size, weight and line height, so the thing that looks like a heading is the thing you click, all the way to the end of the line.

Its label starts where the surrounding text starts: there is no indent, and the chevron sits before the label rather than pushing it inward.
An Accordion therefore lines up with the content above and below it instead of forming a box of its own.

Sections are separated by white space alone, without rules or panels.
The chevron and the heading carry the affordance, which keeps a long list of sections from reading as a stack of boxes.

The chevron turns half a circle when a section opens.
It is animated only for users who have not asked for reduced motion; everyone else sees it arrive already turned.

## Accessibility

Each section renders a heading containing a button that reports whether it is expanded and names the panel it controls.
Screen readers therefore reach the sections by heading, as they would any other outline, and hear the state of each one.

A collapsed panel is removed from the page rather than hidden visually, so its content is not announced, not reachable by keyboard, and — as ‘Find in page’ above explains — not searchable.

The panel is a `section` labelled by its own heading, which makes it a landmark.
This is the reason ‘Reduce landmarks’ offers `sectionAs="div"`: six or more sections put six or more regions in the landmark list, and a landmark per collapsed paragraph tells a screen reader user less than it costs them to walk past.

## See also

- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

<Meta of={ActionGroupStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={ActionGroupStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Both a [Button](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs) and a [Link](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) can provide an ‘action’ in this context.

If two or more Buttons or links are in a row, put the one for the primary action first and the other Buttons behind it.

### How to use

Give the group a name when a page holds several sets of actions and hearing ‘group’ on its own would not say which set this is: point `aria-labelledby` at a heading that names the set, or at text hidden with the `ams-visually-hidden` class.

## Examples

### Stacked

If the Buttons don’t fit next to each other, they will automatically stack vertically and stretch to the full width.
This can occur in a narrow Dialog, with long labels, a large text size, or when zooming in.
Resize the pink rectangle to see this in action.

<Canvas of={ActionGroupStories.Stacked} />

### With Link

An action that involves navigation should be a link.

<Canvas of={ActionGroupStories.WithLink} />

## Features

Putting the primary action first keeps the order of Buttons consistent on both narrow and wide screens: if the Buttons do not fit next to each other, they get stacked vertically with the primary action on top.

## Design

Sighted users will read the primary action first, in line with the natural reading order.
The same goes for users of screen readers, who will hear the primary action first, and users of a keyboard, who will focus the primary action first.

An Action Group places an even gutter between a set of actions, much as a [Row](/docs/components-layout-row--docs) does, and those actions can be [Buttons](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs), [Links](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs), or a mix of the two.
While they fit on one line the group is only as wide as they are, so it can sit at the end of a Dialog or beside other content without claiming the whole line.

The difference from a Row is that an Action Group stretches its actions.
A Row lets each item keep its own width, side by side or wrapped onto new lines when you allow it.
An Action Group makes every action grow to fill the width it has, so the moment they no longer sit in a row they stack into a single, full-width column.
This follows from the space available rather than a breakpoint, as the ‘Stacked’ example shows.

On a shared line, actions are centred against one another, so a Button and a Link of different heights meet on a common middle rather than a top edge.

## Accessibility

An Action Group renders a `div` with the `group` role, so assistive technology presents the actions as one set instead of as unrelated controls that happen to be adjacent.

The group has no name of its own.
Screen readers announce it as a group and then read the actions, which is enough when the page holds only one set; ‘How to use’ covers the case where it is not.

import * as AlertStories from "./Alert.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={AlertStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={AlertStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use an Alert if the message’s purpose matches one of the following:

- **Information** to bring attention to a message.
  This variation is blue and it is the default.
- **Success** to reassure that a process is complete.
  This variation is green.
- **Warning** when action is needed to prevent damage.
  This variation is orange.
- **Error** indicates an error has occurred.
  This variation is red.

### How to use

Place the Alert in a Grid Cell to create enough white space around it.

Important and urgent information is to be placed directly below the Page Header.
Examples: system outage or changes in the opening hours of a City Office.
This can be applied to the entire website or to a part of it.

Add a close button if the user should be able to dismiss the Alert.

Choose a `headingLevel` that fits the outline of the page around the Alert; there is no default.
The heading keeps the size of a level 3 Heading whichever level you pick.

You don’t need to set `headingId`: the Alert generates a unique id for its heading and labels itself with it, so several Alerts on a page never collide.
Pass one only when the heading needs a specific id of your own.

Write the heading and the text so they carry the message on their own.
The severity reaches no one through the colour or the icon alone, which is what [WCAG 1.4.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#use-of-color) asks you to avoid.

## Examples

### Warning

Display a warning when user action is required.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Warning} />

### Error

In case of an error, use the red alert.
Provide the user with suggestions on alternative ways to achieve the goal.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Error} />

### Success

Announce the success of a significant action.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Success} />

### Information

An informative message can emphasize matters that are useful to follow.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Info} />

### With inline link

Include an inline link in the text to guide the user.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.WithInlineLink} />

## Design

An Alert is outlined in the colour of its severity and carries a band of that same colour along its leading edge, with the icon centred in it.
The band takes its dividing line from the outline, so the two meet as one continuous stroke of the same weight.

The background behind the text stays white in all four variants.
Only the outline, the band and the icon change colour, which keeps the text on the same background as the rest of the page and its contrast the same whatever the severity.

The heading is fixed at the size of a level 3 Heading, independent of the `headingLevel` given to it.
Two Alerts then look alike wherever they sit in the outline of a page.

In print, the band keeps its colour rather than being flattened to save ink.
It is the only part told to do so, because without it nothing distinguishes one severity from another on paper.

## Accessibility

An Alert renders a `section` labelled by its heading, which makes it a `region` landmark.
Assistive technology lists it with the other landmarks, so users can reach the message directly instead of hunting for it.

The label is wired up with `aria-labelledby` rather than left to the heading inside.
NVDA in Chrome does not read that heading as the name of the section otherwise.
Setting `headingId` to `null` removes the label, and the landmark with it.

An Alert does not announce itself when it appears.
It is not a live region, so it suits a message that is already there when a view renders rather than one that must interrupt.

The icon carries no text alternative and the severity is conveyed by colour alone, so neither reaches a screen reader.
Both are reinforcement for a message the heading and text already carry, as described under ‘How to use’.

import { Description, Meta, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { PageAnatomy } from "#storybook/_components/PageAnatomy/PageAnatomy";

import { anatomyLabels } from "./anatomyLabels.ts";
import * as ArticleStories from "./ArticlePage.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={ArticleStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={ArticleStories} />

## Anatomy

This schematic shows the default sections for this page type and how the grids and vertical space work.

<PageAnatomy labels={anatomyLabels} of={ArticleStories} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use this page for a single dated article: a news item, a press release, or a blog post.

### When not to use

Use a [News Overview Page](/docs/pages-public-news-overview-page--docs) to list several of them.
Use an [Information Page](/docs/pages-public-information-page--docs) for a topic that stays true rather than one that happened on a date.

## Structure

- The [Breadcrumb](/docs/components-navigation-breadcrumb--docs) has its own [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) to separate its `nav` element from the `main` wrapping the article content.
- The Content Header contains the title, a [Metadata](/docs/components-text-metadata--docs) with the publication date, and the lead paragraph.
- A full-width hero [Image](/docs/components-media-image--docs) separates the Content Header from the body.
  It uses a 16:5 aspect ratio.
- The body ends with a [Link List](/docs/components-navigation-link-list--docs) of related articles.
- A [Spotlight](/docs/components-containers-spotlight--docs) holds a newsletter call-to-action.
- The page closes with a Grid of [Cards](/docs/components-navigation-card--docs) referring to other recent news.

## Layout and spacing

- The Grids use the [recommended Cell sizes](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs#how-to-size-the-grid-cells).
- The [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) utility class sets the vertical space within the Content Header and within the article body.
  Each of those Cells carries the class; the space between them is a padding of the Grid.

## Accessibility

The Breadcrumb takes a Grid above `main`, so its `nav` element stays outside the article rather than reading as part of it.

Two blocks sit outside `main` as well: the newsletter Spotlight and the related articles below it.
Each renders with `as="aside"` and is named by `aria-labelledby` pointing at its own heading, so both reach a screen reader as complementary landmarks that can be skipped to or past.
The headings they point at carry an `id` that exists only to be referenced.

The hero Image and the Card images take an empty `alt`, because the text beside them already says what they show.

## See also

- [News Overview Page](/docs/pages-public-news-overview-page--docs) – lists articles like this one.
- [Spotlight](/docs/components-containers-spotlight--docs) – the call-to-action band, and what its contents need.
- [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs) – the values behind the section above.

<Description of={AvatarStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Show an Avatar for the user of the website, or to associate a person with a content item.

### How to use

On a page in another language, set `initialsAccessibleName` and `userAccessibleName` so the Avatar is announced in that language rather than in Dutch.
Each replaces the entire announcement and is used verbatim, so repeat the initials in `initialsAccessibleName` when they should still be spoken.

## Examples

### With image

The Avatar can also display a photo or other image for the person.
Make sure to scale the image down to around 100 pixels to prevent unnecessary data transfers.
The center of the image will be visible; provide a square image if possible.

<Canvas of={AvatarStories.WithImage} />

### Fallback icon

A user icon displays if no label and image are provided.

<Canvas of={AvatarStories.FallbackIcon} />

## Design

The Avatar contains 1 or 2 initial letters from the person’s full name, a picture, or a generic icon.
The component takes the first two characters of the label and sets them in capitals, so the shape stays the same however the name was written.

To personalize the Avatar, the user can be allowed to choose one of the [highlight colours](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs).
The default is purple.
The design system does not define a meaning to any of these background colours.

The circle is sized from the text it holds rather than from a fixed measurement: its width follows the font size and line height of the initials.
An Avatar showing an image drops the border and grows by exactly the space that border and its padding occupied, so both kinds line up at the same size beside each other.

An image is cropped to the circle from its centre and scaled to cover it, whatever proportions it arrives in.
A portrait that is not square therefore loses its edges rather than distorting.

In print, an Avatar keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

An Avatar is announced exactly once, through a line of text that is in the markup but hidden visually.
The initials themselves are marked `aria-hidden`, and an image is given an empty `alt`.

That hidden text defaults to Dutch: ‘Initialen gebruiker’ followed by the initials, or ‘Gebruiker’ when the label is empty.
It is built from the label even when an image is displayed, so an Avatar showing a photograph is still announced by its initials.
Neither wording is fixed: both can be configured, so an Avatar can be announced in the language of the page it sits on.

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### How to write

Let the Badge contain a short text or a number.

Write a label that stands on its own without the colour behind it.
Nothing but the label reaches a screen reader, and a colour is not a message anyone should have to read, which is what [WCAG 1.4.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#use-of-color) asks of you.

## Examples

### With icon

Include an icon when it provides meaning that isn’t obvious from the text alone, or when it helps with quick recognition.
This may be helpful for statuses, alerts, or categories that users look over instead of reading.

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.WithIcon} />

## Design

Use any of the feedback or highlight [colours](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs) for the background.
The default is green.
Red, orange and green are especially useful for showing an error, warning, or success.
However, they can also be combined with the other colours without carrying these meanings.

A Badge is set in bold at the size and line height of body text, and it is padded on the left and right but not above and below.
Its coloured block is therefore exactly as tall as one line of text, so a Badge placed in a sentence or a table cell does not push the lines around it apart.

The corners are square and there is no border.
The colour fills the block, which is what makes a Badge read as a label applied to something rather than as a control to press.

In print, a Badge keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Badge renders a `span` with no role of its own, so its text is read as part of the sentence or the cell it sits in rather than announced separately.

Neither the background colour nor an icon reaches a screen reader; the label carries the whole message on its own.
‘How to write’ covers what that asks of the wording.

<Meta of={BlockquoteStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={BlockquoteStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Quote someone’s literal written or oral text.

Give a Blockquote a width of half or a whole column of text.
Use [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) or [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) to add vertical whitespace around it.

### How to use

If the citation is in a language other than that of the surrounding content, indicate so through the `lang` attribute.
Assistive technology then switches pronunciation for that passage, which is what [WCAG 3.1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#language-of-parts) requires.

## Examples

### Inverse colour

Use the inverse colour if the Blockquote sits on a dark background.
This ensures the colour of the text provides enough contrast.

<Canvas of={BlockquoteStories.InverseColour} />

## Features

The component sets the quotation marks that match the content language, so mark it with the `lang` attribute.
Arabic (`lang="ar"`) gets guillemets (`«` and `»`) and Dutch gets curly double quotes (`“` and `”`); other languages get their own conventional marks.

## Design

A Blockquote is set in bold text, one size larger than body text, with a tighter line height.
This gives a quotation enough weight to stand apart from the running text around it, without needing a border, a background, or an indent.

The quotation marks come from CSS rather than from the content.
Authors cannot forget them or reach for the wrong pair, and the marks follow the language of the quotation.

A Blockquote has no vertical margins of its own.
This makes vertical rhythm a property of the layout rather than of the component, which is why [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) and [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) provide it.

A quotation that runs onto more than one line has its line lengths balanced, so it does not end on a single short word.

Words that are too long for the line are hyphenated rather than left to overflow.
The browser decides where to split them, so the [language of the document](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs#specify-the-language-for-the-entire-document) must be set correctly.

In print, a Blockquote is never split across two pages.

## Accessibility

A Blockquote renders a `blockquote` element, which maps to the `blockquote` role.
The passage is exposed as a quotation rather than as ordinary text, so the meaning does not depend on the quotation marks, which are decoration drawn by CSS.

## See also

- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

## Subcomponents

### Link

Renders both the list item and the anchor.
Set `linkComponent` to integrate with a routing library.

<Canvas of={BreadcrumbLinkStories.Link} />

<Controls of={BreadcrumbLinkStories.Link} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Breadcrumb to show where the current page sits within the hierarchy of the website and to let users navigate between levels.

### When not to use

Don’t use a Breadcrumb on pages that contain forms.
It can distract users from completing the form, or be confused with a progress indicator.

A Breadcrumb should not have more than 5 items.

### How to write

The first item links to the home page, with ‘Home’ as its text.
This applies to Dutch websites as well.

## Design

The items flow as inline text rather than as blocks in a row.
A trail that is too long for the line wraps like a sentence instead of overflowing or scrolling, which is what keeps a Breadcrumb usable on a narrow screen without a separate arrangement for it.

The separator is drawn by CSS, so it can never be forgotten or typed differently from one page to the next.
It is sized in `ex` units, the height of a lowercase letter, so the chevron stays in proportion to the text beside it at every font size.

In a right-to-left writing direction the chevron is mirrored, so it keeps pointing from one item to the next.
See the [localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) for the design system’s writing-direction support.

Links are not underlined until the pointer is over them.
The chevrons already mark where one item ends and the next begins, and underlining every step would turn a single line of text into a row of separate objects.

In print, a Breadcrumb is never the last item on a page and is never split across two.
A trail at the foot of one page with the content it introduces on the next would say nothing.

## Accessibility

A Breadcrumb renders a `nav` around an ordered list, so it is a navigation landmark and the steps keep their order and their number.

The landmark is named by a heading that is hidden visually and hidden from the outline as well.
It gives the navigation a name for anyone listing the landmarks, without adding an entry to the headings of the page.

The separators are backgrounds on empty pseudo-elements, so nothing is announced between one item and the next.

## See also

- [Routing libraries](/docs/docs-guidelines-routing-libraries--docs) – how to integrate links with external routing libraries.

## Subcomponents

### Cell

Positions content in the Breakout grid through its `colSpan`, `colStart`, `rowSpan`, and `rowStart` props.
Use `as` to change the HTML element.

<Canvas of={BreakoutCellStories.Cell} />

<Controls of={BreakoutCellStories.Cell} />

## Usage guidelines

The Cell containing the Spotlight must have `has="spotlight"` to extend to the gaps and margins around it.
This prop can only be used on Cells that span all columns of the grid, so `span="all"` is required as well.

The Cell containing the figure must have `has="figure"` to ensure it aligns to the bottom.

The content that does not break out defines the height of the Spotlight.
Ensure that the text is short, or the image tall, to prevent losing the break-out effect.

On narrower screens, let the text move below the image.

Write the Cells in the order the content should be read, and use `colStart` and `rowStart` only to decide where each one sits.
Reading order and keyboard order follow the markup rather than the grid, so the two disagree as soon as a start value is used to reorder rather than to place.

## Examples

### Vertical layout

A large figure can be placed at the top of the Spotlight, with related text positioned underneath.

<Canvas of={BreakoutStories.VerticalLayout} />

## Features

This component is an extension of [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs).
It offers the same props, although `span` and `start` have been renamed to `colSpan` and `colStart`.
Additionally, Breakout allows cells to span multiple rows.

## Design

A Breakout Cell escapes the Grid by pulling itself outward by exactly the space the Grid puts around it: the margin at each side, and the vertical gap above and below.
The Spotlight inside it then reaches both edges of the window, while every other Cell keeps to its columns.

The vertical offsets are written out for each gap size, since each one cancels a different amount.
The horizontal offsets simply follow the margin the Grid ends up with.
So when that margin grows to clear a display cutout, the Spotlight still reaches the edge of the screen, and the content beside it moves clear of the cutout.
Each side is cancelled on its own, so a cutout at one edge never pulls the Spotlight away from the other.

Row spans and row starts are generated up to four.
A higher number produces no rule at all rather than an error, so a Cell asking for five rows quietly spans one.

The Cell holding the figure aligns to the bottom of its row, where every other Cell aligns to the top.
That is what lets a tall image sit on the base line of the Spotlight and rise out of the top of it.

## Accessibility

A Breakout renders the same markup as a Grid and adds nothing to the accessibility tree.
Cells are announced in the order they appear in the markup, whatever the grid does with them on screen, and ‘Usage guidelines’ covers what that asks of the markup.

## See also

- [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) – the base layout this component extends.
- [Spotlight](/docs/components-containers-spotlight--docs) – the container that Breakout breaks out of.
- [Figure](/docs/components-media-figure--docs) – the typical content placed inside the break-out Cell.

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Button to start an action, submit a form, or change the state of the interface.

### When not to use

Don’t use a Button to navigate to another page.
Use a [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) or a [Call to Action Link](/docs/components-navigation-call-to-action-link--docs) instead, or an inline [Link](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) in running text.

### How to use

Use only one primary Button per screen.
The primary variant draws attention to the most important action; multiple primaries dilute that signal.

Set `type="submit"` to make the Button submit the surrounding form.

Wrap two or more Buttons or links that sit next to each other in an [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs).

Always provide a short, descriptive label that names the action.
For icon-only Buttons, supply the label through the `children` prop – it is read by screen readers even though it is not shown.

### How to write

Write a short label that names the action.
Use the verb's infinitive form in Dutch, e.g. 'Verwijderen' or 'Opslaan', not 'Verwijder' or 'Sla op'.
Avoid generic labels like 'Klik hier' or 'OK'.

## Examples

### Primary

A primary Button draws attention to the most important call to action.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Primary} />

### Secondary

Use a secondary Button for other actions.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Secondary} />

### Tertiary

Tertiary Buttons distinguish themselves from secondary Buttons when even less emphasis is needed.
They are also the choice for icon-only Buttons.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Tertiary} />

### Disabled

A disabled Button gets a grey background in every variant.
The primary variant uses a darker grey than the secondary and tertiary ones, because its label is white.
Switch off `disabled` to compare the three with their normal appearance.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Disabled} />

### With icon

Add an icon if it makes the Button’s purpose easier or faster to recognise.
The icon appears after the label by default.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIcon} />

### With icon before

The icon can also appear before the label.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIconBefore} />

### With icon only

A Button can consist of just an icon, but only one of our [functional icons](/docs/brand-assets-icons--docs#functional-icons).
You must still provide a label for screen reader users.
If the icon-only Button must align with surrounding text, use an [Icon Button](/docs/components-buttons-icon-button--docs) instead.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIconOnly} />

### Text wrapping

The label may wrap over multiple lines when no shorter text is available, when two Buttons sit next to each other on a narrow screen, or when the user has configured a large font on their device.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.TextWrapping} />

## Features

The Button handles its own focus, hover, active, and disabled states.
On narrow screens or with longer labels, it wraps text without losing alignment.

## Design

The three variants form a hierarchy of importance: primary, secondary, tertiary.
This lets a screen present one clear focal action without ranking every other Button against it.

A label is set at the same size and weight as body text, with a tighter line height of 1.4 against the 1.6 of running text.
Nothing about the type marks a Button as important; its colour and its filled shape do that.

All three variants carry a border of the same width, and the corners are square.
A tertiary Button keeps that border transparent until the pointer is over it, and a secondary Button thickens its outline with an inset shadow rather than a wider border.
Neither changes the space a Button takes up, so a row of Buttons never shifts as one of them is hovered.

Hover styling applies only where a pointer can actually hover.
On a touch screen it would otherwise stay behind after a tap, leaving the Button that was pressed last looking active.

The button overrides the icon’s line height with its own, so the icon sits on the label’s line rather than on a taller one of its own.
The icon keeps its default size, the same body-text size the label uses.
An icon-only Button is square: the icon is given a square box, and the padding is equal on all four sides.

A label that does not fit is hyphenated rather than left to overflow.
The browser decides where to split it, so the [language of the document](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs#specify-the-language-for-the-entire-document) must be set correctly.

In print, a Button keeps its background and border colours instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Button renders a `button` element, which brings keyboard focus, activation with both Enter and Space, and the `button` role with it.

Its `type` defaults to `button` rather than to `submit`.
A Button inside a form therefore leaves that form alone until asked otherwise, which is why submitting takes an explicit `type="submit"`.

An icon-only Button takes its accessible name from the `children` you pass.
That text is rendered in the markup and hidden visually, so screen readers announce the same words a visible label would have carried, and the icon adds nothing to the name.

Disabling a Button with the `disabled` attribute removes it from the tab order, so a keyboard user never lands on it and reads no reason for it being unavailable.
The same appearance applies to `aria-disabled="true"`, which keeps the Button focusable and lets assistive technology announce it as disabled.

## See also

- [Icon Button](/docs/components-buttons-icon-button--docs) – an icon-only button aligned with surrounding text.
- [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) – for navigation to another page.
- [Call to Action Link](/docs/components-navigation-call-to-action-link--docs) – a prominent link styled like a Button.
- [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs) – lays out multiple Buttons and links.
- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

**Note**: `dir` and the navigation and accessible-name labels are read-only here and follow `locale`, so the controls show a fully localised Calendar.
In your own app you set them yourself.

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Calendar to display a month view for content organised by date, such as an event calendar.

### When not to use

Use a [Date Input](/docs/components-forms-date-input--docs) instead when the user needs to select a date in the context of a form.

### How to use

Display the month for the selected date, which may not be the current month.

Give it an accessible name with `accessibleName`.
The Calendar renders this name as a visually hidden heading and generates a unique `id` for it; pass `accessibleNameId` to set that `id` yourself.

#### Localisation

The Calendar renders weekday names, the month caption, and the accessible date labels in the language of `locale`, which defaults to `nl-NL`.
It does not translate the rest: set `accessibleName`, `nextMonthButtonLabel`, `nextYearButtonLabel`, `previousMonthButtonLabel`, and `previousYearButtonLabel` in the same language, or they stay Dutch and screen readers announce a mix.
For right-to-left scripts such as Arabic, also add `dir="rtl"`; this mirrors the layout and the navigation chevrons.
Try the `locale` control above to preview each language; see the [localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) for the tested locales.

If your app uses Calendar in multiple places with the same language, a small wrapper component avoids repeating these props; the [Localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) shows an example.

## Examples

### Dates without links

Each date can be a link, for example to a page that lists that day's events.
`linkTemplate` builds the target for a date; return `undefined` to render the date as plain text, or omit `linkTemplate` entirely to render a plain, non-interactive month.

<Canvas of={CalendarStories.DatesWithoutLinks} />

## Features

### Routing library integration

Pass `linkComponent` to let a router supply its own link element, such as the one from Next.js.
Use it together with `linkTemplate`.
For more details, see the [routing libraries guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-routing-libraries--docs).

This example for a `linkTemplate` function produces links like `?date=2026-12-04` for 4 December 2026:

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```ts
const formatDate = (date: Date) =>
  `${date.getFullYear()}-${String(date.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, "0")}-${String(date.getDate()).padStart(2, "0")}`

const linkTemplate = (date: Date): string => `?date=${formatDate(date)}`
```

### Custom navigation icons

Different navigation icons can be used through the `*ButtonIcon` props, which each take the same value as the [Icon](/docs/components-media-icon--docs) component’s `svg` prop.
Websites for the City of Amsterdam must use the default icons.
For right-to-left scripts, give a custom icon a `data-directional="true"` attribute so it mirrors like the default chevrons; see the [localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs).

## Design

The month is laid out as seven equal columns, one per weekday, so the dates line up in vertical columns whatever month is shown and however long the weekday names are.

The grid shows only the days of the month on view, padding the first week with blank cells rather than the previous month’s tail.
Our palette has no comfortable way to mark another month’s dates as secondary, and without that a second set of the same day numbers would read as noise rather than context.

The Calendar is only as wide as it needs to be, up to a set width, and never wider than the space it is given.
It can therefore sit in a narrow column beside other content without a layout deciding its size for it.

The month caption is centred between the navigation buttons rather than placed beside them, so moving from one month to the next does not shift it.

Today is marked by weight alone: no box, no background, no colour of its own.
Dates that are links keep the ordinary link colour, so the marking for today does not compete with the marking for what can be followed.

Navigation chevrons mirror in a right-to-left layout, which is why a custom icon needs to say that it is directional.

## Accessibility

The Calendar renders as a `nav` landmark.
Screen readers announce each link with its full date, including the weekday, so a day number is never read out of context.

The name of that landmark comes from `accessibleName`, rendered as a heading that is present in the markup and hidden visually.

A month whose dates are not links is a plain grid of text.
Nothing in it is focusable, so it is read as content rather than offering a keyboard user a month of stops to pass through.

## See also

- [Date Input](/docs/components-forms-date-input--docs) – lets the user select a date in the context of a form.

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Call to Action Link to guide the user to a page where they can perform an action.

### When not to use

A single page must not have more than one Call to Action Link.
Ensure the emphasis is on one product, and divide the content into several pages if needed.

For additional guidelines, refer to the [Link](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) component.

Use [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) or [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) to add vertical whitespace.

### How to write

Use the verb's infinitive form, such as "Kapotte parkeerautomaat melden", not "Meld kapotte parkeerautomaat".

## Design

The Call to Action Link features a green background to ensure it stands out.
To clarify that it is not a button, which is not suitable for navigation, its text is underlined like links typically are.
This informs users that a new page will open and that they can either copy the link or open it in a new window.

Green is not used for a [Button](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs) anywhere in the system, so the colour marks the difference as much as the underline does.

The corners are square and the vertical padding is slight, so the block hugs its line of text.
It reads as a highlighted link rather than as a large control, which is the distinction the underline is there to protect.

Because the block itself stays small, the space around it does the work of drawing the eye.
It takes an [x-large space](/docs/docs-guidelines-vertical-space--docs) above and below it, where the body text it sits among takes medium, so it reads as the one action of the page rather than as another paragraph in the flow.
[Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) applies that space; outside a Prose container, set it with the `ams-mb-xl` [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) utility class on the Call to Action Link and on the element above it.

In print, it keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Call to Action Link renders an `a` element, so it is announced as a link and listed among the links of the page, however much it looks like a button.

Someone who navigates by pulling up a list of links finds it there rather than among the controls, and hears where it goes rather than what it would do.
That is the distinction the underline makes visually and the element makes for everyone else.

## See also

- [Link](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) – for inline links in running text.
- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

## Subcomponents

### Image

The image of the Card.
It accepts all props of a regular [Image](/docs/components-media-image--docs), such as `aspectRatio` or a set of image sources.
Only use decorative images with `alt=""` here.
The heading provides screen reader users with enough context.

<Canvas of={CardImageStories.Image} />

<Controls of={CardImageStories.Image} />

### Heading

Contains the name and link of the Card.
Accepts all props of a regular [Heading](/docs/components-text-heading--docs).
Set its `level` to fit the document outline.

<Canvas of={CardHeadingStories.Heading} />

<Controls of={CardHeadingStories.Heading} />

### Heading Group

Displays a [Metadata](/docs/components-text-metadata--docs) above the heading.
Write it after the Heading; the component reverses the two, so a screen reader reaches the heading first.

<Canvas of={CardHeadingGroupStories.HeadingGroup} />

<Controls of={CardHeadingGroupStories.HeadingGroup} />

### Content

Groups everything in a Card that is not its image.
Add it whenever you want to allow switching to a [horizontal layout](#horizontal-layout).

### Link

Makes the entire Card clickable.
Place it inside the Heading.
Set `linkComponent` to integrate with a routing library.

<Canvas of={CardLinkStories.Link} />

<Controls of={CardLinkStories.Link} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

A Card needs more content than just a title.
Add a short text and optionally an image and metadata.

### When not to use

This component is not the best option if the target content does not represent an article-like page.
In that case, use a Heading, a Paragraph and a [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) instead.

### How to use

Card Heading requires a `level`, because there is no sensible default.
The guidelines for regular [links](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) and [headings](/docs/components-text-heading--docs) apply.

Give a Card one link and no more.
The Card Link covers the whole Card to make it clickable, so a second link inside it would sit underneath and be impossible to click.

### How to write

Place the text in a regular [Paragraph](/docs/components-text-paragraph--docs).
Use a small [Metadata](/docs/components-text-metadata--docs) for a publication date or a category.

## Examples

### With metadata

A Card can show a category, a date, or both above its heading.
Wrap the Heading in a Heading Group and add a [Metadata](/docs/components-text-metadata--docs) after it, at the small size.

<Canvas of={CardStories.WithMetadata} />

### Horizontal layout

A Card can place content beside the image once there is room for it.
This follows the width of the nearest [query container](/docs/utilities-css-query-container--docs), so the same Card is horizontal in a wide Grid Cell and vertical in a narrow one, without any change to the markup.
A Card that has an image but no Content subcomponent stays vertical.

If the Card spans 9 columns of the Grid, the image covers 4 of them.
In other contexts, the image scales proportionally.

The example below is vertical in a narrow window.

<Canvas of={CardStories.HorizontalLayout} />

### Top tasks

A set of cards without images can present links to frequently accessed interactions.
A short title and description are enough to guide the user to the page they need.
Position 4 to 8 tasks on a [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs); left-align them and do not skip cells.
For a group of links without a description, use a [Link List](/docs/components-navigation-link-list--docs) instead.

<Canvas of={CardStories.TopTasks} />

## Features

The mandatory title of a Card is a link within a Heading.
The link is made active across the entire area of the Card.

A Card that pairs an image with a Content lays out horizontally once its container is wide enough, and vertically below that.

## Design

A Card has no border, no background, and no padding.
It is a stack of parts with white space between them, so a row of Cards reads as a set of articles rather than as a row of boxes.

The whole Card is made clickable by stretching an invisible layer from the link across it.
Only the title is the link, and everything else stays plain content, so the target grows without the accessible name growing with it.

The focus ring is drawn around the entire Card instead of around the title alone, and the link’s own ring is switched off.
Browsers that cannot express that condition get neither rule, so they still show the ordinary ring on the title rather than nothing at all.

In a Heading Group the Metadata is written after the heading and displayed above it.
The reading order and the visual order differ on purpose, which is what lets the metadata sit on top while the heading is still what gets read first.
Writing it before the heading undoes both.

Whether a Card is horizontal follows the width of its container rather than the width of the window.
The same Card is one row in a list of results and one card in a row of three, and which of the two it should be depends on the space it is given, not on the size of the screen.

The image of a horizontal Card measures 4 of the 9 columns it spans, which is the width of a vertical Card beside it, and it keeps its aspect ratio rather than stretching to the height of the text beside it.
Both choices exist so that the image is the same size in either direction: an index page that opens with a row of vertical Cards above a list of horizontal ones then has one left edge and one image width running down it.
Stretching the image instead would crop each one differently, according to how far its heading happened to wrap.

## Accessibility

Visually, Card Heading has the size of a level 3 Heading by default.
Screen reader users can navigate by heading or by link; a Card supports both because its title is a heading that contains a link.
A screen reader reads the title first, then the rest of the content.

The layer that makes the Card clickable is empty and carries no text, so it adds nothing to the name of the link and is not announced.
The rest of the Card stays ordinary content: a paragraph inside it is read as a paragraph, not as part of the link.

An image in a Card is decoration, which is why the examples pass an empty `alt`.
A description there would be read when browsing the page but skipped when moving between links, so it would reach some readers and not others.

## See also

- [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) – for a single link to a follow-up page when a Card is too much.
- [Skeleton](/docs/components-feedback-skeleton--docs) – can increase the perceived performance of loading the Card’s content.
- [Routing libraries](/docs/docs-guidelines-routing-libraries--docs) – how to integrate links with external routing libraries.

<Title />

<Description of={CharacterCountStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Only use a Character Count when there is a good reason for limiting the number of characters users can enter.
For example, if there is an indication that users are likely to enter more information than they need to.
Or when there is a legal or technical reason that means an entry must be no more than a certain number of characters.

### When not to use

If your users keep hitting the character limit imposed by the backend of your service then try to increase the limit rather than use a Character Count.

## Examples

### Error

When the length exceeds the maximum length, the colour of the text changes to red.

<Canvas of={CharacterCountStories.Error} />

### Translated text

The component displays its text in Dutch by default.
Pass one of the exported formatters – or a custom function – to `formatText` to display the count in another language.
The Arabic formatter applies Arabic number–noun agreement.
See the [Localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) for the tested locales.

<Canvas of={CharacterCountStories.Translated} />

## Features

Users will get updates at a pace that works best for the way they interact with the textarea.
This means:

- sighted users will see a count message that updates as they type;
- screen reader users will hear the count announcement when they stop typing.

This component does not restrict the user from entering information.
The user can enter more than the character limit, but are told they’ve entered too many characters.
This lets them type or copy and paste their full answer, then edit it down.

## Design

A Character Count is one line of small text below the field.
It keeps the ordinary text colour instead of being greyed down, so a reader who needs to check the count is not asked to read weaker text than the rest of the form.

Going over the limit turns it red, and that is the whole of the change: no icon, no border, and nothing about the field itself.

Counting up towards the limit rather than down from it means the message says the same thing before and after the limit is passed.
The wording never has to switch from characters remaining to characters too many.

## Accessibility

A Character Count is a status region, so screen readers announce the new count without moving focus and without interrupting what is being read.
Someone typing hears the count between words rather than after every keystroke, which is what ‘Features’ above describes.

The text is fixed Dutch — the count, the word ‘van’, the limit, and ‘tekens’ — and cannot be configured.
That is worth weighing before using a Character Count on a page in another language.

Going over the limit is signalled by colour alone, so the count itself has to be read for the change to register.
The text says the same thing either way, which is what keeps the message complete without the colour.

<Meta of={CheckboxStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={CheckboxStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use Checkboxes for one or multiple choices that do not exclude each other.
Each Checkbox operates independently of other Checkboxes in a list at the same hierarchical level.
Checking an additional Checkbox does not affect other selections in that list.

Use a Checkbox to answer a closed question if multiple answers are possible.

Use a group of Checkboxes to filter data on a page, in a menu, or within a component.

A Checkbox can also be used for bulk selection or deselection of an entire list of Checkboxes.
Still, it should be clear that the bulk selection Checkbox is at a different hierarchical level than the list being fully selected or deselected.

### When not to use

Use a [Radio](/docs/components-forms-radio--docs) when a user can select only one option from a list.

### How to use

Wrap a list of Checkboxes in a Field Set with a legend describing what the list is about.
For example, if the Checkboxes are used to get answers to a question, the legend is the question.

### How to write

A label starts with a capital letter.
It does not have punctuation at the end if it is a single sentence, word, or fragment.
It is written in the first person when asking the user to agree to the terms and conditions.

## Examples

### Long label

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.LongLabel} />

### Disabled

A disabled Checkbox fills its square to show it is unavailable.
Switch on `checked` or `indeterminate` to see that a selected disabled Checkbox keeps its darker fill, so the mark stays legible.

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.Disabled} />

### In a Field Set

Use a Field Set to group several Checkboxes with a legend, description and / or an Error Message.

Because of an [NVDA bug](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718), we add the description text to the Field Set with `aria-labelledby`,
instead of `aria-describedby`.
Screen reader users will no longer be able to skip the description, but we think that is preferable to missing the description entirely.
The order of the `id`s is the order in which they are read by screen readers.

If you don’t need the description, remove its Paragraph and the `aria-labelledby` and `id` attributes from the Field Set.

Do not use rich text (such as links or lists) in descriptions. [Find out why](/docs/components-forms-field--docs#no-rich-text).

Check [the Field Set docs](/docs/components-forms-field-set--docs) for more information on configuring it.

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.InAFieldSet} />

### In a Field Set with validation

A Field Set with Checkboxes can become invalid.
In this case, connect an Error Message to the Field Set.
Because of [the NVDA bug mentioned earlier](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718),
we add the Error Message text to the label as well.
Add an `aria-labelledby` attribute to the Field Set and provide the `id` of Error Message as its value.
The order of the `id`s is the order in which they are read by screen readers.

Do not use rich text (such as links or lists) in an Error Message. [Find out why](/docs/components-forms-error-message--docs#no-rich-text).

Check [the Field Set docs](/docs/components-forms-field-set--docs) for more information on configuring it.

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.InAFieldSetWithValidation} />

### With custom icon

Replace the icon with a custom version to use the Checkbox in a different theme or visual identity.
Use `ams-checkbox__rectangle`, `ams-checkbox__hover-indicator`, `ams-checkbox__checked-indicator`
and `ams-checkbox__indeterminate-indicator` classes in its SVG markup.
Websites for the City of Amsterdam must use the default icon.

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.WithCustomIcon} />

## Design

A list of Checkboxes is vertically stacked to enhance readability and usability.

The box is drawn as an SVG inside the label rather than by the browser, which is what makes a custom icon possible at all and keeps the control identical across browsers.
It carries a separate ring that appears on hover, so the box grows a halo instead of changing size or colour.

The box and the label sit in one line box that never breaks between them, and the label may wrap onto as many lines as it needs beside it.

Checked, indeterminate, invalid and disabled each change one thing: the fill, the mark inside, the outline colour, or the text colour.
The states can therefore combine — an invalid checked box, a disabled indeterminate one — without any pair of them fighting over the same property.

In forced colours mode the drawing is redone in system colours: the box takes the field colours, a selected one the active text colour, and a disabled one the greyed text colour.
The fills the tokens set are ignored there, so without this a checked box and an empty one would look the same.

## Accessibility

A Checkbox renders a native `input` inside a `label`, so the whole label is the target and the browser supplies the role, the checked state and the keyboard behaviour.

The input is not hidden away: it is reduced to no width, which keeps it focusable, announced, and submitted with the form.
Its focus ring is moved onto the label so the ring surrounds the box and its text rather than a control with no size.
Browsers without support for the modern focus rules show that ring for every focus, including a click, which is the safer way round.

The indeterminate state is a visual and programmatic state of the checkbox itself, not a third value.
A form submits it as unchecked, so a bulk-selection box in that state says something about the list below it and nothing about its own value.

The invalid styling responds to `aria-invalid="true"` and to the browser’s own `:invalid` state alike.

## See also

- [Radio](/docs/components-forms-radio--docs) – when a user can select only one option from a list.
- [Field Set](/docs/components-forms-field-set--docs) – groups several Checkboxes with a shared legend.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/column.tokens.json";

import * as ColumnStories from "./Column.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={ColumnStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={ColumnStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Wrap a Column around a set of elements that need the same amount of white space between them.

### When not to use

Do not use a Column for text – various types of elements require different amounts of space between them.
Wrap editorial content in the [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) utility class to have all spacing set automatically.

To add white space below a single element, use [Margin Bottom](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) instead.

### How to use

Give a Column a name when you set `as="section"`.
A `section` reaches assistive technology as a landmark only once it has one, so give the heading inside it an `id` and point `aria-labelledby` at that id.
Without a name the element groups the content in the markup but adds nothing anyone can navigate to.

## Examples

### Alignment

Items in the column can be aligned vertically in several ways:

- **Center**: center items within the column.
- **End**: align items to the bottom of the column – to the bottom.
- **Space Between**: distribute whitespace between items.
- **Space Around**: distribute whitespace around items.
- **Space Evenly**: distribute whitespace evenly around items.

By default, items align to the **start** of the column – at the top.
This option has no class name or prop value.

This example centers three items vertically.

<Canvas of={ColumnStories.Alignment} />

### Horizontal alignment

Items in the column can be aligned horizontally in several ways:

- **Start**: align items to the start of the column. This is the left side in left-to-right languages.
- **Center**: center items within the column.
- **End**: align items to the end of the column. This is the right side in left-to-right languages.

This example centers three items horizontally.

<Canvas of={ColumnStories.HorizontalAlignment} />

### Improve semantics

By default, a Column renders a `<div>` element in HTML.
Use the `as` prop to make your markup more semantic.
In this example, the Column uses a `<section>` element to group the heading and the cards.

<Canvas of={ColumnStories.ImproveSemantics} />

## Features

Five sizes of [space](/docs/brand-design-tokens-space--docs) are available for the width or height of the gap.
The medium gap is the default.

Align the elements horizontally or vertically through the alignment props.

## Design

The gap is the only spacing a Column provides.
There is no padding, no margin, and no divider between items, so the space belongs to the container and the items keep whatever spacing they define for themselves.

All five gaps scale with the width of the window rather than stepping at a breakpoint.
The white space in a layout therefore grows in proportion with the type and the grid around it, instead of holding still until a threshold is crossed.

Every item in a Column gets the same gap, which is why ‘When not to use’ steers editorial text towards [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs).
A heading needs less space above the paragraph it introduces than below the one before it, and a single gap cannot express that.

## Accessibility

A Column renders a `div` by default, which adds nothing to the accessibility tree.
Its items are announced exactly as they would be without it, in the order they appear in the markup.

The `as` prop can render an `article` or a `section` instead, which does reach assistive technology.
‘How to use’ covers what a `section` needs before it becomes a landmark.

## See also

- [Row](/docs/components-layout-row--docs) – stacks its children horizontally instead.
- [Spacing](/docs/docs-guidelines-spacing--docs) – which tools to use for white space and when.

<Meta of={DateInputStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={DateInputStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Date Input when the user must enter a calendar date and the date picker provided by the browser is appropriate.

### When not to use

When asking for a date that is easy to remember or find, like a birthday or passport expiration date,
use a Field Set with separate Text Inputs for day, month, and year.
This approach is easier to use than using a Date Input component.

For more information on this pattern, see the [gov.uk](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/) and [NL Design System](https://nldesignsystem.nl/richtlijnen/formulieren/wanneer-welk-form-element/iedereen-kan-invullen) documentation.

Avoid disabling input fields.
They cause usability and accessibility problems.
Disabled fields are often skipped by screen readers.
This makes it hard for users who rely on assistive technologies to understand the form’s content.
They are not included in form submissions, which can lead to incomplete or missing data.

Alternatives:

1. Use the `readonly` attribute.
   This makes a field uneditable but keeps it accessible and included in form submissions.
2. Display data as plain text or within a non-input element like a `span` or `div`.
3. Use conditional logic to hide or show fields based on user interaction.
   This ensures all necessary fields are accessible and editable when needed.
4. Use a label or text to explain why a field is not editable if you must disable it temporarily.
   This helps the user understand the context.

### How to use

Wrap a Date Input in a Field to associate it with a Label, description, and Error Message.

## Examples

### Memorable date

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.MemorableDate} />

### Memorable date with validation

To show validation errors, add `invalid` and an [Error Message](/docs/components-forms-error-message--docs) to the Field Set.
Make sure to connect the Error Message to the Field Set, otherwise this won’t be read by a screen reader.
Additionally, apply the `invalid` prop to the Text Inputs to visually indicate the error.
Only use the `invalid` prop on Text Inputs that have errors.
For example, only mark the ‘year’ input as invalid if the year is not provided.

See the [gov.uk](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/#error-messages) documentation on validation for this pattern.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.MemorableDateWithValidation} />

### Date and time

To let the user select a specific time on a date, use the `datetime-local` type.
Note that the control’s UI varies in general from browser to browser.

The value represents a local date and time, not necessarily the user’s local date and time.
In other words, the input allows any valid combination of year, month, day, hour, and minute – even if such a combination is invalid in the user’s local time zone.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.DateTime} />

### Invalid

Indicates that the input value does not meet the specified constraints.
An [Error Message](/docs/components-forms-error-message--docs) must be displayed above the field.
To highlight the error even more, the parent [Field](/docs/components-forms-field--docs) component’s `invalid` prop must also be set.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.Invalid} />

### Disabled

A field that cannot (yet) be used takes a grey background, and its value greys out with it.
It will not respond to interactions, e.g. with the mouse or keyboard.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.Disabled} />

### In a Field

Use a Field to group a Date Input with a Label, description and / or an Error Message.

If you don’t need the description, remove its Paragraph and the `aria-describedby` from the Date Input.

Check [the Field docs](/docs/components-forms-field--docs) for more information on configuring it.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.InAField} />

### In a Field with validation

If the Date Input can become invalid, add an Error Message and its `id` to the `aria-describedby` attribute of the Date Input.

Check [the Field docs](/docs/components-forms-field--docs) for more information on configuring it.

<Canvas of={DateInputStories.InAFieldWithValidation} />

## Design

This component uses a native date input, which is styled differently in different browsers and operating systems.
Recreating the native functionality is quite difficult and prone to accessibility errors, which is why we’ve chosen not to do that.
This does mean that this component does not look identical on all browsers and operating systems.

The styling therefore stops at the box: the border, the padding and the type are ours, and the segments inside it, the format hint and the calendar that opens belong to the browser.
Chromium lets its calendar button be replaced, so there it carries our icon; other browsers keep their own.

The field is given a minimum width and height.
A native date field is much smaller when empty than when filled on some devices, and without a floor a form would visibly resize as it was completed.

Everything else — the border, the padding, the type, and the invalid and disabled states — matches a [Text Input](/docs/components-forms-text-input--docs), so a date sits level with the other fields of a form.

## Accessibility

A Date Input renders a native `input` of a date type, so screen readers announce it segment by segment and every browser’s own keyboard handling applies: arrow keys to change a part, typing to fill one, and the browser’s picker for those who prefer it.
That behaviour is the reason for using the native control rather than rebuilding it.

The format the field shows and expects comes from the browser and the operating system, not from the language of the page.
A visitor whose browser is set to another locale sees the order of day, month and year they are used to, which is helpful — but it also means the page cannot promise which one they will see.

The invalid styling responds to `aria-invalid="true"` and to the browser’s own `:invalid` state alike.
The second matches a partially entered date as well, so a field can turn red while someone is still filling in its segments; set `aria-invalid` from your own validation to control when that happens.

## See also

- [Calendar](/docs/components-navigation-calendar--docs) – navigate between dates using a calendar view.
- [Field](/docs/components-forms-field--docs) – wraps a single input with its Label, description, and Error Message.
- [Field Set](/docs/components-forms-field-set--docs) – use with three Text Inputs for memorable dates instead of a Date Input.
- [Time Input](/docs/components-forms-time-input--docs) – the counterpart for entering a time.

**Note**: Some props are excluded from the controls panel: `mode`, `onChange`, and `value` are managed by the story’s state wrapper; `defaultMonth`, `isDateDisabled`, `maxDate`, and `minDate` have no suitable control widget for their type.
The `dir` and the navigation and accessible-name labels are read-only and follow `locale`, so the controls show a fully localised Date Picker; set them yourself in your app.

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Date Picker when someone needs to choose a date or date range from a visible calendar, for example to book an appointment.

### When not to use

- Use a [Date Input](/docs/components-forms-date-input--docs) when the user knows the date and can type it into a form field.
- Use a [Calendar](/docs/components-navigation-calendar--docs) to browse content grouped by date, such as an events calendar.

### How to use

The Date Picker is a controlled component: it keeps no selection of its own.
Pass the current selection with `value` and update it in the `onChange` handler.

In the default single mode, `value` is a `Date` or `null` and `onChange` receives the picked date.
In range mode, set `mode="range"`; `value` is a `DateRange` (`{ start, end }`) and `onChange` receives the updated range.
The first pick sets the start, the second sets the end, and picking before the start begins a new range.

If you set `minDate` or `maxDate`, ensure the initial `value` falls within those bounds.
The component does not clamp or validate the incoming value.

#### Localisation

The Date Picker renders weekday names, the month caption, and the accessible date labels in the language of `locale`, which defaults to `nl-NL`.
It does not translate the rest: set `nextMonthButtonLabel`, `nextYearButtonLabel`, `previousMonthButtonLabel`, and `previousYearButtonLabel` in the same language, or they stay Dutch and screen readers announce a mix.
In range mode, also localise `rangeStartAccessibleName` and `rangeEndAccessibleName`; they are appended to the start and end dates when those are announced.
For right-to-left scripts such as Arabic, also add `dir="rtl"`; this mirrors the layout and the navigation chevrons.
Try the `locale` control above to preview each language; see the [localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) for the tested locales.

If your app uses Date Picker in multiple places with the same language, a small wrapper component avoids repeating these props; the [Localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs) shows an example.

## Design

The Date Picker is intentionally an inline component.
Finding the optimal date is a focused task for the user; placing it directly on the page makes it easier to use and gives it the space and attention it deserves.
If the layout truly has no room, placing the Date Picker inside a [Modal Dialog](/docs/components-containers-modal-dialog--docs) is an acceptable last resort.

## Examples

### Range

Set `mode="range"` to let users pick a start and end date.
The Date Picker itself does not communicate that a range is expected.
Use a label, heading, or instruction to make this clear.

The user picks the start date first.
A second click on a later date completes the range; clicking the same date completes a one-day range.
Clicking a date before the current start discards the selection and begins a new range from that date.
Any click after the range is complete starts over.

<Canvas of={DatePickerStories.Range} />

### Disabled dates

Pass `isDateDisabled` to prevent selection of specific dates, such as ones that are unavailable.
Disabled dates remain reachable with the keyboard and are announced, but they cannot be selected.

<Canvas of={DatePickerStories.DisabledDates} />

### Within-month bounds

Use `minDate` and `maxDate` to bound the selectable period.
Dates outside the range cannot be selected, and the month and year navigation buttons stop at the edges of the range.

When the bounds fall within the current month, dates outside them appear disabled: they are struck through and cannot be selected, but remain reachable by keyboard.

<Canvas of={DatePickerStories.WithinMonthBounds} />

### Limited to one month

When `minDate` and `maxDate` align with month edges, all dates remain selectable.
Only the navigation buttons are disabled.

<Canvas of={DatePickerStories.LimitedToOneMonth} />

## Features

### Keyboard navigation

The day grid follows the [WAI-ARIA grid pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/).
Arrow keys move between days, Home and End jump to the start and end of the week, and Page Up and Page Down move between months; hold Shift for years.
Enter or Space selects the focused day.
Moving past the end of a month shows the adjacent month and keeps focus on the day.

### Custom navigation icons

Different navigation icons can be used through the `*ButtonIcon` props, which each take the same value as the [Icon](/docs/components-media-icon--docs) component’s `svg` prop.
Websites for the City of Amsterdam must use the default icons.
For right-to-left scripts, give a custom icon a `data-directional="true"` attribute so it mirrors like the default chevrons; see the [localisation guide](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs).

## Design

The Date Picker is intentionally an inline component: the calendar sits directly in the page, not in a dropdown or popover opened from a field or button.
Finding the optimal date is a focused task for the user; placing it directly on the page makes it easier to use and gives it the space and attention it deserves.
If the layout truly has no room, placing the Date Picker inside a modal [Dialog](/docs/components-containers-dialog--docs) is an acceptable last resort.

A date that falls outside the bounds is struck through rather than removed or greyed into the background.
It keeps its place in the grid, so the shape of the month stays intact and the reason a date cannot be chosen is visible rather than inferred from a gap.

The grid shows only the days of the month on view; the first week is padded with blank cells rather than the previous month’s tail.
Our palette has no comfortable way to mark another month’s dates as secondary, and without that a second set of the same day numbers — two 1sts, two 30ths — would confuse more than it clarifies.
Showing them would also raise a question the inline grid is better without: if someone picked a day carried in from a neighbouring month, should the grid jump to that month? Leaving those days out avoids it.

## Accessibility

The grid takes its accessible name from the visible month caption, so screen readers announce which month is shown.
Each day button is labelled with its full date, including the weekday, so a day number is never read out of context.
In range mode, the start and end dates are announced as such; override `rangeStartAccessibleName` and `rangeEndAccessibleName` to localise these.

Dates that cannot be chosen stay reachable with the keyboard and are still announced.
Someone moving through the month therefore learns which days are unavailable instead of finding the grid silently skip over them.

The month names, weekday names and spoken dates follow `locale`, while the navigation labels do not.
‘Localisation’ under ‘How to use’ lists the ones you have to set yourself, and leaving them unset is what produces the mix of two languages a screen reader would read out.

## See also

- [Date Input](/docs/components-forms-date-input--docs) – lets the user type a known date into a form field.
- [Calendar](/docs/components-navigation-calendar--docs) – displays content organised by date in a month view.

import * as DescriptionListStories from "./DescriptionList.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={DescriptionListStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={DescriptionListStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Subcomponents

The Term, Description, and Section subcomponents make up a Description List.
Term and Description render the `<dt>` and `<dd>` elements, and a Section groups a term with its descriptions.
None of them has props of its own; the examples on this page show them in place.

## Usage guidelines

## Examples

### Orientation

Resize the following example to see the Description List adapt its layout to the available width.

<Canvas of={DescriptionListStories.Orientation} />

### Multiple descriptions

A term can have several descriptions.
Descriptions have the same spacing as sections because they usually include longer text.

<Canvas of={DescriptionListStories.MultipleDescriptions} />

### Multiple terms

If several terms have the same description, place them in a `DescriptionList.Section` component for a correct grid layout.
The terms are positioned closely together.

<Canvas of={DescriptionListStories.MultipleTerms} />

### Multiple terms and descriptions

Do not group multiple terms with several descriptions.
This type of content is too complicated and will distort the layout.
Use distinct sections instead, or find an alternative to a Description List.

### Rich description

A description can include rich content such as inline formatting, links, paragraphs, and even lists.

<Canvas of={DescriptionListStories.RichDescription} />

### Inverse colour

Use the inverse colour if the Description List sits on a dark background.
This ensures the colour of the text provides enough contrast.

<Canvas of={DescriptionListStories.InverseColour} />

## Design

The terms and descriptions stack vertically by default.
They sit next to each other when their [query container](/docs/utilities-css-query-container--docs) is wide enough (at least `32rem`).

The column for the terms is as wide as the longest term, without wrapping.
Its width can be adjusted to ‘wide’ (50%), ‘medium’ (33%), or ‘narrow’ (20%), which also allows the terms to wrap.

Terms use heading typography and descriptions use body text, which gives the two different line heights.
Side by side, a term therefore gets half of that difference as extra space above it, so its first line sits level with the first line of its description.

The term is set in bold text, and its line lengths are balanced so it does not end on a single short word.

## Accessibility

A Description List renders `dl`, `dt`, and `dd` elements.
These tie each term to its descriptions in the markup instead of only through the layout, which is the kind of relationship [WCAG 1.3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#info-and-relationships) asks to be made available.
A Section renders a `div` around one group, which HTML permits inside a `dl`.

Screen readers expose description lists in noticeably different ways: the number of items they report, the context they give for a term or a description, and the commands available to move through the list all vary.
The component leaves the native elements alone rather than adding `term` and `definition` roles, because overriding them changes how VoiceOver announces the list.

## See also

- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.
