# Typography

We have a fluid typography system.
The options for the font family, font size, line height and font weight come in two groups: body text and headings.

## Body text

### Font size

The size of text adjusts to the width of the window for pleasant reading on screens of any size.

| CSS variable                                        | ≤&nbsp;320 | Example                                                                                                  | ≥&nbsp;1440 | Example                                                                                                  |
| :-------------------------------------------------- | :--------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-small-font-size)`   |     16     | <TypographySample fontSize="1rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-small-line-height)" />      |     16      | <TypographySample fontSize="1rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-small-line-height)" />      |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-font-size)`         |     18     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.125rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />        |     20      | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />         |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-large-font-size)`   |     21     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.3125rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-large-line-height)" /> |     25      | <TypographySample fontSize="1.5625rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-large-line-height)" /> |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-x-large-font-size)` |     24     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.5rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-x-large-line-height)" />  |     32      | <TypographySample fontSize="2rem" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-x-large-line-height)" />    |

### Line height

The line heights have been designed to match the corresponding font size.
Do not combine tokens of different sizes.

| CSS variable                                          | Value |
| :---------------------------------------------------- | :---: |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-small-line-height)`   |  1.5  |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)`         |  1.6  |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-large-line-height)`   |  1.5  |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-x-large-line-height)` |  1.4  |

### Font weight

The font weight can be light, regular, bold, extra bold, or black.

| CSS variable                                             | Value | Example                                                                                                                                                              |
| :------------------------------------------------------- | :---: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-light-font-weight)`      |  300  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-light-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />      |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-font-weight)`            |  400  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />            |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-bold-font-weight)`       |  700  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-bold-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />       |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-extra-bold-font-weight)` |  800  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-extra-bold-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" /> |
| `var(--ams-typography-body-text-black-font-weight)`      |  900  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-black-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-body-text-line-height)" />      |

None of our components use the light, extra bold, or black weight yet.
You can apply any of these to a component of your own by referencing its token as the `font-weight`.
Reserve the black weight for short, prominent display text; it is much heavier than bold.

## Headings

### Font size

We support five sizes for headings, although levels 1 to 4 are most commonly used.

| CSS variable                                | ≤&nbsp;320 | Example                                                                                                                                                   | ≥&nbsp;1440 | Example                                                                                                                                                   |
| :------------------------------------------ | :--------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-1-font-size)` |     32     | <TypographySample fontSize="2rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-1-line-height)" />      |     48      | <TypographySample fontSize="3rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-1-line-height)" />      |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-2-font-size)` |     24     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.5rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-2-line-height)" />    |     32      | <TypographySample fontSize="2rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-2-line-height)" />      |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-3-font-size)` |     21     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.3125rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-3-line-height)" /> |     25      | <TypographySample fontSize="1.5625rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-3-line-height)" /> |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-4-font-size)` |     18     | <TypographySample fontSize="1.125rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-4-line-height)" />  |     20      | <TypographySample fontSize="1.25rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-4-line-height)" />   |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-5-font-size)` |     16     | <TypographySample fontSize="1rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-5-line-height)" />      |     16      | <TypographySample fontSize="1rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-5-line-height)" />      |

### Line height

Headings use smaller line heights than body text.

| CSS variable                                  | Value |
| :-------------------------------------------- | :---: |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-1-line-height)` |  1.2  |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-2-line-height)` |  1.3  |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-3-line-height)` |  1.3  |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-4-line-height)` |  1.4  |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-5-line-height)` |  1.4  |

### Font weight

Headings only use the bold font weight.

| CSS variable                                | Value | Example                                                                                                                                                   |
| :------------------------------------------ | :---: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)` |  700  | <TypographySample fontSize="1.5625rem" fontWeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-font-weight)" lineHeight="var(--ams-typography-heading-3-line-height)" /> |

## Other aspects

### Font family

All text appears in our Amsterdam Sans font.
If it is not available, we use Arial or the generic sans-serif instead.

| CSS variable                        |                Value                |
| :---------------------------------- | :---------------------------------: |
| `var(--ams-typography-font-family)` | 'Amsterdam Sans', Arial, sans-serif |

### Font style

Text is upright by default, but can be set in italics as well.

| CSS variable                              | Value  | Example                                                                  |
| :---------------------------------------- | :----- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var(--ams-typography-italic-font-style)` | italic | <TypographySample fontStyle="var(--ams-typography-italic-font-style)" /> |

### Hyphenation

Words that do not fit on a single line will be split with a hyphen and continue on the next line.
We let the browser decide when and how to hyphenate words.
This is why it is important to [set the correct language](/docs/docs-guidelines-localisation--docs#specify-the-language-for-the-entire-document) for the website.

| CSS variable                                  | Value |
| :-------------------------------------------- | :---- |
| `var(--ams-typography-hyphenate-limit-chars)` | auto  |

### Underlining

We only underline hyperlinks.
To see how, consult our [tokens for links](/docs/brand-design-tokens-links--docs).

### Letter spacing

Kerning has been optimized in the font file.
We do not adjust the space between glyphs.

## Compact Mode

Our large font sizes for public websites would be counterproductive in internal websites.
They use [Compact Mode](/docs/docs-guidelines-modes--docs), where both body text and headings are considerably smaller.

<Meta title="Pages/Introduction" />

# Pages

This section demonstrates how to compose pages with the Design System’s components.
It uses the latest versions of the libraries, without any customizations.
This gives an honest representation of what they can achieve and how they work in the browser.

## Documentation

We offer examples for various page types; see the list in the sidebar.
We separate templates for public websites from those for internal ones.

The ‘Docs’ page for each page explains its design decisions and how to build it.

## Examples

The ‘Default’ example shows the actual page in its entirety.
Some page types have more than one example.

### Flexible content

Reload an example to get new random texts and images.
Use the ‘Control’ tab to see how it looks with your own content.

### Test for accessibility and see HTML output

The ‘Accessibility’ tab offers a report of various automatic tests.
The ‘HTML’ tab displays the entire document as rendered by all components on the page.

### Check how the page would look on various devices

The buttons in the toolbar offer various features, of which the ‘three-layered square’ button replicates the appearance and behaviour of the page on a phone, tablet or desktop.
Press the button with the two arrows to rotate the screen.

### See the page full-screen

Use the ‘Go to full screen’ (or press `alt+F`) or ‘Open canvas in new tab’ buttons to the top right to see the entire page.

<Meta title="Pages/Guidelines/Choosing a page type" />

# Choosing a page type

Start from what the page is for rather than from what it looks like.
Two questions settle most of it: is the site public or internal, and does the page carry content, help someone find content, or carry a task?

## Public pages that carry content

The [Article Page](/docs/pages-public-article-page--docs) presents a single news item, from its headline and lead to the related reading that follows.
The [Information Page](/docs/pages-public-information-page--docs) explains a topic that is neither a product nor a news article, for a reader who wants to understand something rather than arrange it.
The [Product Page](/docs/pages-public-product-page--docs) brings together everything a resident needs to know about a product or service of the City, and guides them toward the next step.
The [Project Page](/docs/pages-public-project-page--docs) keeps residents and stakeholders informed about a construction or traffic project.
The [Profile Page](/docs/pages-public-profile-page--docs) presents a single person, group of people, or place.
The [Handbook Page](/docs/pages-public-handbook-page--docs) presents long-form reference material as a set of short pages that stay easy to navigate.

## Public pages that help people find content

The [Home Page](/docs/pages-public-home-page--docs) is the entry point of a website, offering a broad overview of its main topics, common tasks, and recent news.
The [Navigation Page](/docs/pages-public-navigation-page--docs) is a signpost with little content of its own, grouping links to related pages.
The [News Overview Page](/docs/pages-public-news-overview-page--docs) lists content items that a visitor narrows down with filters.
The [Events Overview Page](/docs/pages-public-events-overview-page--docs) lists dated activities instead, adding a calendar and date facets for visitors who arrive with a date in mind.
The [Search Results Page](/docs/pages-public-search-results-page--docs) presents what a visitor finds after searching the site, in that same filter-and-results layout.
The [Loading Page](/docs/pages-public-loading-page--docs) shows how such a page behaves while it fetches its content.

## Public pages that carry a task

The [Form Flow](/docs/pages-public-form-flow--docs) guides the user through a task one step at a time, with a stripped-back header and footer that keep the focus on answering each question.

## Internal pages

The [Home Page](/docs/pages-internal-home-page--docs) is the entry point of an internal website, such as a backoffice system.
The [Navigation Page](/docs/pages-internal-navigation-page--docs) suits websites whose content is organised into a handful of main sections that each have their own subsections.
The [Table Page](/docs/pages-internal-table-page--docs) helps users work through large sets of data, with the sorting, filtering, and paging state kept in the URL.

## When none of these fits

Most new page types turn out to be an arrangement of sections these templates already use, so [Composing your own page](/docs/pages-guidelines-composing-your-own-page--docs) is the place to start.
Where your context needs something else, design it, and tell us about it: templates that prove themselves in a service are candidates to join the design system.

import { Meta } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

<Meta title="Pages/Guidelines/Page structure" />

# Page structure

Every page template is built from the same shell.
This page gives that shell for both contexts, and the rules that hold for any page inside it.

## A public page

```tsx
<Page>
  <SkipLink href="#inhoud">Direct naar inhoud</SkipLink>
  <PageHeader>
    <Grid />
  </PageHeader>
  <Grid>
    <Breadcrumb />
  </Grid>
  <main id="inhoud">
    <Grid>{/* the Content Header */}</Grid>
    <Grid>{/* the body */}</Grid>
  </main>
  <PageFooter>
    <PageFooter.Spotlight>
      <Grid />
    </PageFooter.Spotlight>
    <PageFooter.Menu />
  </PageFooter>
</Page>
```

Public websites cannot use the [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) component.
They should offer navigation using the Page Header only.

## An internal page

```tsx
<Page withMenu>
  <SkipLink className="ams-page__area--skip-link" href="#inhoud">
    Direct naar inhoud
  </SkipLink>
  <PageHeader className="ams-page__area--header" noMenuButtonOnWideWindow>
    <Menu />
  </PageHeader>
  <Menu className="ams-page__area--menu" inWideWindow />
  <main className="ams-page__area--body" id="inhoud">
    <Grid />
  </main>
  <PageFooter className="ams-page__area--footer" />
</Page>
```

All children of `Page` have a class name starting with `ams-page__area--` to lay them out correctly on the underlying grid.

Internal websites may use a [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) to support navigation across major functional areas or modules.
This pattern helps users move efficiently between different parts of the website while keeping the structure clear and predictable.

The component must be rendered twice.

1. One instance, for narrow and medium windows, sits in the Page Header.
   The user can access it through the menu button.
   Hide the menu button on wide windows: this instance hides itself there, so the button would open an empty menu.
2. A second Menu goes between the Page Header and the main content.
   This is for wide windows, where the menu is positioned to the side.
   The `inWideWindow` prop ensures that only one of both components is present at all times.

Make sure that both menus have the same items.

## Landmarks

A landmark is not always a section itself.
The Content Header is a section of its own, so a content page wraps its sections in a `main` element, or places `main` in a Grid Cell beside a sidebar.
A page that is a single section — a question page of a Form Flow, for instance — sets `as="main"` on that Grid instead.
Such a wrapper takes no padding of its own, and the Grids inside and around it keep theirs.

The [Breadcrumb](/docs/components-navigation-breadcrumb--docs) takes a Grid of its own above `main`, so that its `nav` element stays outside the main landmark.

## The skip link

Every page opens with a [Skip Link](/docs/components-navigation-skip-link--docs) targeting `#inhoud`, which is the `id` of the `main` element.
The shared layout of these templates renders it, so a template itself only has to provide the `main` it points at.

## Headings on a page

The page title is a level 1 [Heading](/docs/components-text-heading--docs#sections-and-blocks), and the sections below it are level 2.

On a public page, a Heading below the title keeps the size of its level where it introduces a content body, and takes a `size` one step smaller where it introduces a block or a group of blocks.
Most sections are groups of blocks, so on all but the content page types every heading under the title takes the smaller size.

Internal pages leave every heading at the size of its level.
Compact Mode already sets the type down a step, and a second reduction would leave too little between a section and the block inside it.

## See also

- [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs) – where the space between these sections comes from.
- [Page](/docs/components-containers-page--docs) – the outermost wrapper.
- [Page Header](/docs/components-containers-page-header--docs) – the top of every page.
- [Page Footer](/docs/components-containers-page-footer--docs) – the bottom of every page.

<Meta title="Pages/Guidelines/Layout and spacing" />

# Layout and spacing

Laying out a page is a lookup rather than a judgement call.
This page gives the values; a template’s own documentation page only records where it departs from them.

## Vertical space between sections

Between the Page Header and the Page Footer, the Page holds a sequence of sections.
Most sections are a Grid, but a section can also be a Spotlight, an Image, or an Overlap.
A Spotlight contains a Grid, which in that position also spaces the content against the edges of the coloured band.

Sections create this space with the padding props of the Grid.
A section that is not a Grid has no padding props and takes its space from the Grids around it.
The Page Header and the Page Footer add no vertical space of their own, so the first and the last Grid provide it.

Internal pages give every Grid the same `paddingVertical` of `x-large`.
The sequence below applies to public pages, which vary the padding along the page.

### The first Grid

The first Grid has a `paddingTop` of `large` and no `paddingBottom`.
On most pages it contains only the Breadcrumb, and on the question pages of a Form Flow only the back link.

Not every page type has a breadcrumb.
A page deep in a handbook relies on its table of contents instead, for one.
Where the first Grid holds content instead of a breadcrumb, it still takes the `large` top padding.

A page may also open with a section that is not a Grid.
The Home Page starts with an Overlap, which sits flush against the Page Header.
The Grid that follows such a section is a regular one, with a `paddingVertical` of `x-large`.

Only the Breadcrumb closes the gap below itself.
The back link keeps the regular `x-large` between itself and the section that follows.

### The Content Header Grid

The Grid that follows the Breadcrumb holds the Content Header: the page title, an optional [Metadata](/docs/components-text-metadata--docs), and the lead paragraph.
It has no `paddingTop`, so that the breadcrumb and the page title read as a single block.
Its Cell carries the [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) utility class, which spaces those three as [vertical space](/docs/docs-guidelines-vertical-space--docs) recommends.
The body Cells of these templates use it too, so a page template sets no bottom margins of its own within a Cell.

Its `paddingBottom` depends on what meets the boundary on either side of it.
Where both this Grid and the one below it have the default background colour, it takes `2x-large`, which sets the Content Header apart from the body that follows.
Where either of them meets that boundary with a full-width band — a Spotlight, or an Image or Image Slider spanning the whole Grid — `x-large` is enough, because the edge of that band marks the boundary already.
It makes no difference which of the two the band belongs to: a Grid that ends in one takes `x-large` below it as much as one that is followed by a coloured section does.

An image that shares its row with text, as the lead image does on the Information Page, is not such a band: the default background still runs along the boundary beside it, so the Grid keeps its `2x-large`.

A page that opens with a search rather than with prose puts its Search Field in that same Cell, in the place of the lead.
Prose then spaces it a medium below the title, as it does the lead.
Where the field wants to be narrower than the documented Cell, so the input does not stretch to an unusable length, the whole Content Header Cell narrows with it.

Anything larger — an Image Slider, for one — takes a Grid Cell of its own instead, and the row gap of `x-large` sets it apart from the title above it.

### The Grids in between

Every remaining Grid uses a `paddingVertical` of `x-large`, including the Grid inside a Spotlight.

Two adjacent Grids therefore add up to twice that amount.
Across a Spotlight this is intentional, because the coloured band separates the two paddings.
Between two plain Grids, leave the padding off one of the touching sides, unless the extra whitespace is deliberate.

### The last Grid

The last Grid before the Page Footer has a `paddingBottom` of `2x-large`.

A last section that is not a Grid has no Grid after it to take its space from.
Give it the `ams-mb-2xl` [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) utility class instead, for the same amount of space.

A page that needs only one Grid combines both rules: a `paddingTop` of `large` and a `paddingBottom` of `2x-large`.

### Vertical gaps

Usually, leave `gapVertical` at its default of `x-large`.

## Space inside a Grid Cell

The [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) utility class sets the space between most types of elements of a Cell, following the [vertical space](/docs/docs-guidelines-vertical-space--docs) recommendations.
A Cell that carries it needs little bottom margins of its own.

Where Prose has no rule for an element, every element but the last sets its own bottom margin with an [`ams-mb-*`](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) utility class, in the amount the vertical space guide gives.

### Spacing a section heading

A heading in a Cell of its own is spaced by the row gap of the Grid, which is an `x-large` where the guidance asks for a `small` or less.

Give that Grid a `gapVertical` of `none`, let the heading Cell set the right amount with an `ams-mb-*` utility, and put the Cells below it in a [Grid Subgrid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs#subgrid) with a `gapVertical` of `x-large`, which is the gap the Grid used to give them.
A section that shares its Grid with the Content Header needs a Grid of its own first, since the header depends on that row gap.

## How to size the Grid Cells

Almost everything on the page is wrapped in a [Grid Cell](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs).
Its `span` and `start` props let you define where all sections go on the page.
Do so for all variants of the Grid (narrow, medium, and wide: 4, 8, and 12 columns).

Some typical page sections always use the same values:

### Content Header

The Content Header contains the page title, an optional Metadata with the publication date or the taxonomy tags, and the lead paragraph.
It is a bit **wider** than the body section and is positioned slightly further **to the left**.

```tsx
<Grid.Cell span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 7, wide: 9 }} start={{ narrow: 1, medium: 1, wide: 2 }} />
```

Breadcrumbs use their own Grid placed directly above the Content Header, using the same cell configuration.
See [the Content Header Grid](#the-content-header-grid) for the space around and inside this section.

### Content Body

The body section contains the main textual content of the page.
It spans **7 columns** on the wide grid and **6 columns** on the medium-wide grid to maintain an optimal line length for readability.
This also applies to forms.

```tsx
<Grid.Cell span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 6, wide: 7 }} start={{ narrow: 1, medium: 2, wide: 3 }} />
```

### Side-by-side blocks

Link Sections (a block with a heading, paragraph, and standalone link) can be displayed **side by side**, for example within a Spotlight.
Two of them take half the wide grid each, and the `start` prop is not needed.

```tsx
<Grid.Cell span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 4, wide: 6 }} />
```

Where a set of blocks sits under a heading of its own, put them in a [Grid Subgrid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs#subgrid) spanning the whole Grid.
The Subgrid hands its columns to its own Cells, so each block is placed against the columns of the page without repeating a `start`, and the heading above keeps a Cell in the Grid itself.

```tsx
<Grid>
  <Grid.Cell span="all">{/* the heading */}</Grid.Cell>
  <Grid.Subgrid gapVertical="x-large" span="all">
    <Grid.Cell span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 4, wide: 3 }} />
  </Grid.Subgrid>
</Grid>
```

Where those blocks hold the same kind of thing – Cards, news items, search results – the set is a list.
Give the Subgrid `as="ul"` and each Cell inside it `as="li"`.
Keep whatever is not one of the items outside it, such as the heading or a Pagination.
[Semantic list of cards](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs#semantic-list-of-cards) shows how.

Where two columns run beside one another and one is much taller, give **each column** its own Subgrid instead.
A Subgrid is a single item in the row of the Grid however many rows it holds, so the columns stack independently rather than a tall block pushing its neighbour down.
On the narrow grid the second column then lands below the whole of the first rather than interleaving with it.

```tsx
<Grid>
  <Grid.Subgrid span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 4, wide: 5 }} start={{ narrow: 1, medium: 1, wide: 2 }} />
  <Grid.Subgrid span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 4, wide: 5 }} />
</Grid>
```

Blocks placed straight into a Grid rather than a Subgrid still need a `start` on every other Cell to hold the left-hand column, which is worth avoiding where a Subgrid will do.

### Top tasks

Top-task overviews use Cards that contain only a heading and a paragraph, without an image.
On the wide grid, each Card spans 3 columns, fitting **4 per row**.
On the narrow and medium-wide grids, each Card spans 4 columns.
The `start` prop is not needed here.

```tsx
<Grid.Cell span={{ narrow: 4, medium: 4, wide: 3 }} />
```

### Preview cards

Index pages such as news overviews or search results use Cards as well for navigation.
They usually do include the image of the target content.
These layouts require **4 columns** for each Card, which can be achieved with a single spanning value:

```tsx
<Grid.Cell span={4} />
```

## See also

- [Vertical space](/docs/docs-guidelines-vertical-space--docs) – the space between any two components.
- [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) – the component that carries all of this.
- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – the utility that spaces the contents of a Cell.
- [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) – the utility classes for everything Prose does not cover.

# Reading the anatomy

The ‘Docs’ page of each page type opens with a schematic of its Default example, drawn once per Grid variant: the narrow, medium, and wide grids of 4, 8, and 12 columns.
It reads the sections and the cells on them from the example itself, so it shows the same page.

Side by side, the three drawings share one scale.
The vertical space between the sections is the amount the tokens give it, and each square of the paper is one [`ams.space.m`](/docs/brand-design-tokens-space--docs): 16 pixels on a phone and 24 on a desktop.
The height of a cell is an impression: nothing in the example says how tall its content is.
It comes from a scale of seven steps, from a single line of text to a body of one, so the same kind of content is the same size on every page type and nothing is drawn taller than a body of text.
Where there is no room for three drawings beside one another, the buttons above them choose which of the three to show.

## Repeated cells

A page often repeats one cell down a whole screen, such as the eight top tasks of a home page.
The drawing shows the first row of such a run and the last, with a dashed marker in between for the ones it leaves out.
That marker counts cells where they lie one under the other, and rows where they lie beside one another: ‘8 more’, but ‘3 × 2 more’ for three rows of two.
It all happens per Grid variant, because a run that fills a phone from top to bottom may take two rows on a desktop.

# Composing your own page

Most page types turn out to be an arrangement of sections these templates already use.
Build a page we do not list by naming its bands and looking up what each one takes, and invent where your context asks for something the set does not cover.

## The sections a page is made of

Walk your design from top to bottom and name each band as one of these:

- A **breadcrumb**, in a Grid of its own above the main landmark.
- A **content header**: the page title, an optional metadata line, and the lead paragraph.
- A **body**: the running text of the page, in a cell narrow enough to read comfortably.
- **Side-by-side blocks**: any number of short blocks that each end in a link.
- **Top tasks**: a row of Cards with a heading and a paragraph, and no image.
- **Preview cards**: Cards that do carry the image of the page they point at.
- A **Spotlight band**: a full-width coloured band, usually holding a call to action.
- A **full-bleed image**: an Image or Image Slider that runs to the edges of the page.

Naming the bands is the design decision.
Everything after it is a lookup in [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs).

## The order to decide in

1. **Public or internal.** They differ in mode, in navigation, and in how the padding varies down the page.
2. **Content, findability, or a task.** See [Choosing a page type](/docs/pages-guidelines-choosing-a-page-type--docs) for what each group looks like.
3. **One column, or a body beside a sidebar.**
4. **Which sections, top to bottom**, in the vocabulary above.
5. **Look up** the Cell sizes and the Grid padding. Do not measure the design.

## A variant is often enough

A page that differs from an existing template in its content rather than its structure is usually a variant of that template.
The [Profile Page](/docs/pages-public-profile-page--docs) covers a person, a group and three kinds of place in one template, which saves reaching for something new each time the subject changes.

Where your context genuinely calls for a page type we do not have, design it.
The sections above are there so it comes out consistent with the rest, not to keep the set closed.

We would like to see it either way.
A page type that works in one service usually works in others, and templates that prove themselves are candidates to join the design system.
Tell us what you built and what you had to invent for it, and we will look at taking it on.

## See also

- [Page structure](/docs/pages-guidelines-page-structure--docs) – the shell every page shares.
- [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs) – the values each section takes.
- [Reading the anatomy](/docs/pages-guidelines-reading-the-anatomy--docs) – how to read the schematics.

# Public websites

The City maintains numerous websites for various target audiences: citizens, entrepreneurs and visitors.
This section presents a number of page types for websites of which Amsterdam is the primary sender, and the intended audience is the general public or a specific part of it.

## Spacious Mode

Public websites must use the default Spacious Mode, which applies generous
[typography](/docs/brand-design-tokens-typography--docs) and [spacing](/docs/brand-design-tokens-space--docs).
This appearance keeps the focus on the content.
It makes information easy to read and helps users find what they need without distractions.

## What sets these pages apart

Public websites cannot use the [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) component.
They should offer navigation using the Page Header only.

They also vary the vertical padding along the page, where an internal page gives every Grid the same amount.
Both differences are covered where the rules are: [Page structure](/docs/pages-guidelines-page-structure--docs) and [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs).

## See also

- [Choosing a page type](/docs/pages-guidelines-choosing-a-page-type--docs) – what each of these page types is for.
- [Page structure](/docs/pages-guidelines-page-structure--docs) – the shell every page shares.
- [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs) – the Grid padding and the Cell sizes.
- [Internal websites](/docs/pages-internal-introduction--docs) – the page types for backoffice systems.

# Internal websites

The design system also supports internal websites, such as backoffice systems used by our staff.

These typically require higher information density and faster task execution.
The guidelines below describe how to apply the design in these contexts.

## Compact Mode

Internal websites frequently use [Compact Mode](/docs/docs-guidelines-modes--docs), which applies reduced sizes for [typography](/docs/brand-design-tokens-typography--docs) and [spacing](/docs/brand-design-tokens-space--docs).
This mode increases information density and improves the use of available screen space.

Compact Mode automatically adjusts all components.
As a result, they remain consistent and equally suitable for task-oriented workflows as they are for content-driven public websites.

## What sets these pages apart

Internal websites may use a [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) beside the page, which a public website cannot.

They also give every Grid the same `paddingVertical` of `x-large`, where a public page varies that padding along the page.
Both differences are covered where the rules are: [Page structure](/docs/pages-guidelines-page-structure--docs) and [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs).

- [Layout and spacing](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs) – the Grid padding and the Cell sizes.
- [Public websites](/docs/pages-public-introduction--docs) – the page types for the City’s public sites.
